newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Abkhazians cut Georgia power in tit-for-tat row.
newsitem.headline: Abkhazians cut Georgia power in tit-for-tat row.

text.p: Separatists in Georgia's breakaway region of Abkhazia have cut off power supplies from the country's main hydroelectric plant, apparently retaliating for the severing of phone lines out of the separatist region.
Energy ministry officials in the Georgian capital Tbilisi said the absence of electricity from the Inguri hydro station would force Georgia to import power from Russia and Azerbaijan.
"This is against international norms," Deputy Energy and Fuel Minister Revaz Arveladze told Reuters.

Inguri, a gigantic socialist-era monolith, is designed to provide three billion killowatt-hours of electricity yearly and has accounted for around 50 percent of Georgia's power over recent years as imports of natural gas and fuels become costly.
The station straddles the de facto border between Abkhazia and Georgia. The dam facilities are in territory controlled by Georgia, while generating works are over the river in Abkhazia.
Georgia and Abkhaz separatists fought a bitter war in 1992-93 when Georgia sent troops to crush an independence drive.
The separatists routed government troops in a year of fighting and have since run the region as a de facto independent state. Peace talks are deadlocked and the situation is tense.
Arveladze said Inguri was due to undergo a major three-month overhaul from later this month.
Georgia already suffers massive power shortages in winter due to a lack of cash to pay for imports and a poor payment collection system from consumers.

Tbilisi officials said the Abkhaz government had taken the action in retaliation for Georgia's insistence that the region's inter-city and international phone lines, which previously had gone via Russia, be cut off.
Georgian Communications Minister Phridon Indzhia said the government had managed to convince Russia to cut off Abkhazia's remaining 48 phone lines this week.
He said the Black Sea region, with an estimated population of 200,000, now had only a handful of satellite lines for emergency use by government officials.
Indzhia said Georgia had offered to connect Abkhazia to the Georgian phone grid but Abkhazia had declined. The Abkhaz have said the cable leading to Georgia is damaged beyond repair.
"We prepared everything so that Abkhazia could route its phone connections through Georgia, but they did not take advantage of this," Indzhia told Reuters.
